speakers: Patrick (Pat) Welton (guest; founder and CEO, Welton Investment Corporation; physician)
summary: Pat Welton (Welton Investment Corp, ex-Commodities Corp trader) on 40 years of managed futures: trend, systematic macro, short-term flow and relative-value sleeves. Trend returns decompose into economic carry, financial carry, information diffusion and reflexivity; volatility targeting fixed fast-reversal losses; capacity is detected via execution costs. Regimes change which data matter; investor return gap from performance chasing is the biggest cost.

coverage.note: nothing new: cold-open quote (recorded in C03), intro, Welton biography
Commodities Corp history; capital allocated to traders as return targets are hit
Tudor Jones lessons: exiting at size depends on liquidity; counterparty also believes in an edge; rest is firm-building anecdote
allocator vs investor risk needs (target vol vs opportunity-scaled exposure), prop trader RAROC, early program's variable volatility
losses 3-4x faster on reversals before vol targeting, vol targeting adoption, savvy investor flows as drawdown-end signal, performance chasing, trend's portfolio value
manager drift from marketing feedback, four seminal manager questions, agnostic multi-asset edge, convexity/skew at quarterly horizon
four S framework (setup, signal, sizing, symmetry); discipline of following one's own system; narrative remarks not recorded
replication as price-signal smoothing, minimal market set replicates the trend industry, replicating the replicators performs better
cost and manager-selection failure points, behavioral basis of trending and non-trending periods, four-component trend return decomposition, opposing equity carries

fixed income trend returns = term premia, 2013-14 rates episode, zero correlation and convexity via attribution, carry vanishes at short horizons, flows drive <10-day returns, short-term trend rarely works
strategy separation by data type, neutralized relative-value baskets, risk-off sleeve on hedging-flow data, underallocation to alternatives, multistrats not hurting trend
ZIRP and narrow G7 spreads hurt trend, multistrat arbitrage provides liquidity, trend as tail tool for quarter-to-year adverse moves
industry capacity thought experiment, many approaches converge to average, long-term trend less capacity-sensitive, style-drift constraint, market impact, execution-cost capacity monitor
per-market liquidity limits (copper vs tin), execution-delay sensitivity test, unstable data-surprise to price mapping; Alan's regime question
which data matter changes by regime (money supply), trade differently in supply- vs demand-constrained regimes, investor return gap; closing and outro

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: we were allocated more money every quarter as we hit return targets.
claims.claim: Commodities Corporation, an early multistrategy pod shop, scaled each trader's capital up quarterly as they met return targets, a performance-contingent allocation rule.
claims.direction: more capital to traders hitting targets
claims.testable: partly - allocation rule across sleeves can be simulated but no rule details given

claims.speaker: Pat Welton (quoting Paul Tudor Jones)
claims.quote: when you start trading size, you can't only think about getting out when you want. you have to get out when the market lets you.
claims.claim: At large size, exit timing is constrained by available market liquidity, so liquidity must be part of position planning, not only the signal.
claims.conditions: matters once position size is large relative to market liquidity
claims.testable: partly - market impact / exit cost can be modelled vs position size and volume

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: markets weren't math. That there's somebody on the other side of every single trade who at that moment believes they also have an edge.
claims.claim: Markets are not a mathematical system but a set of counterparties each believing they have an edge, so market structure and who is on the other side matter for any edge.
claims.testable: no - general principle

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: if they're more like an allocator than an investor, they might want something that is more consistently exposed and more constant and targeted volatility
claims.claim: Allocators who slot a manager into a portfolio want constant exposure and a targeted volatility, so risk management should be designed around the client's goals.
claims.testable: partly - fixed vs variable vol targeting can be compared, but client preference is not testable

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: if they were more of an investor, they might want more exposure when there's a better value or when there's a better forward return profile and less exposure when it's weaker
claims.claim: Investor-type clients prefer exposure scaled to expected forward return (more when value/opportunity is better, less when weaker) instead of constant risk.
claims.direction: raise exposure when forward return is higher
claims.testable: yes - opportunity-scaled vs constant-vol sizing can be backtested

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: most prop traders for themselves are probably thinking something on the order of a ray rock, right? A riskadjusted rate of return on capital. So they think in dollars more than they think in percents.
claims.claim: Proprietary traders optimise risk-adjusted return on capital in dollars, while managers of outside money must optimise in percentage terms for the client's goals, which changes the sizing formula.
claims.testable: no - framing difference

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: its average volatility would be in in well approximately probably about a 15v in the '9s but that might be 10 v when there's less opportunity and 20 when there's more
claims.claim: Welton's 1990s diversified medium-term trend program ran variable volatility around 15% average, roughly 10% with less opportunity and 20% with more, i.e. risk scaled with opportunity.
claims.direction: higher risk when more trend opportunity
claims.testable: yes - variable (10-20%) vs fixed 15% vol trend portfolio can be compared

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: rising volatility which oftentimes accompanied by rising correlation that the overall net exposure was rising and that it wasn't poor timing but that a reversal in some cases was approximately three or four times faster in equity P&L
claims.claim: Without volatility targeting, rising volatility plus rising correlation inflated net portfolio risk, so trend reversals lost money about three to four times faster than gains accrued.
claims.indicator: realized volatility; cross-asset correlation; drawdown speed vs gain speed
claims.direction: losses faster than gains without vol scaling
claims.testable: yes - compare loss vs gain speed of vol-targeted and unscaled trend backtests

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: in the early 2000s, many people including ourselves began volatility targeting the portfolio or volatility targeting segments of the portfolio
claims.claim: Volatility targeting of the whole portfolio or of its segments mutes the fast-reversal losses and makes trend more compatible with professional allocators.
claims.testable: yes - portfolio-level vs segment-level vol targeting can be backtested

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: when they would call and double the size of their account. I was almost certain that that was the end of any industry draw down.
claims.claim: Skilled investors added to managed futures near the end of industry drawdowns and cut near the end of good runs, so their contrarian flows timed the strategy cycle.
claims.indicator: allocations by savvy investors into CTAs
claims.direction: add after drawdowns, trim after strong runs
claims.conditions: only for a few savvy investors
claims.testable: partly - CTA drawdown-buy rule testable; investor flows not observable

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: It's the usual tragedy of managed money to watch people watch performance, wait for there to be enough confirmation and confidence, get in a little bit too late and put themselves on a right shift of time off cycle.
claims.claim: Most investors wait for performance confirmation before allocating to managed futures, so they enter late and are systematically out of phase with the return cycle.
claims.testable: yes - fund flow vs subsequent return (dollar- vs time-weighted) can be measured

claims.speaker: Niels
claims.quote: I think our industry as trend followers it's probably not the most uh liked uh investment strategy out there but it offers tremendous value
claims.claim: Pure trend following has an unattractive standalone return shape but adds large value inside a traditional portfolio.
claims.conditions: as an addition to a traditional portfolio
claims.testable: yes - portfolio with and without trend allocation can be compared

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: one of the most pernitious and damaging things I think traders have done to themselves is to respond to marketing feedback in the hopes of growing their business. They end up changing what they do.
claims.claim: Managers who change their strategy in response to client/marketing feedback drift from their market edge and get worse results; the test should always be whether a market edge exists.
claims.testable: partly - style drift vs later performance could be studied across managers

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: the four seminal questions were always, what's your edge in the marketplace? How and where are you going to exploit that edge? What is your risk management or position sizing?
claims.claim: A trader or strategy should be evaluated on four questions: its edge, where/how it exploits it, its risk management/sizing, and how it protects its tails.
claims.testable: no - evaluation checklist

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: You offer them the possibility as capital moves from one asset class to another, from one subasset group to another, from long to short, from long to flat
claims.claim: Pure trend following's edge comes from agnostic multi-asset, multi-directional participation, capturing returns as capital rotates between asset classes, sub-groups and from long to short or flat.
claims.testable: yes - compare long-only/single-asset vs multi-asset long-short trend

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: You are picking up return as that capital moves over months and quarters. It brings the convexity that is so valuable. It brings the skew that's so valuable at least on the time frame of quarterly and semiannually
claims.claim: Trend following delivers positive convexity and positive skew mainly at quarterly and semiannual horizons, not necessarily at shorter measurement intervals.
claims.testable: yes - skew of trend returns at monthly vs quarterly vs semiannual frequency

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: Two, second S, what's your signal? What makes you get in? What makes you get out? Three, what's your sizing? This is sort of synonymous with risk management, but um sizing now includes forward opportunity and risk.
claims.claim: A systematic strategy should define four S's: setup (conditions raising probability), signal (entry/exit), sizing (forward opportunity and risk) and symmetry (asymmetric win/loss).
claims.testable: no - design framework

claims.speaker: Pat Welton (quoting John Henry)
claims.quote: the difference between our success and other people's is that we actually follow our system
claims.claim: Edges persist even when rules are public because others lack confidence to follow a system that is not theirs; discipline in following the system is what captures the edge.
claims.testable: no - behavioral claim about implementers

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: That's really replicating the actions of others through the reflection of the information of the price signal which is then typically smoothed and brought in.
claims.claim: Trend following is itself a form of replication (smoothing prices that reflect others' actions), so replicating another manager's P&L via regression is a small further step and a valid method.
claims.testable: yes - regression replication of CTA index returns

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: what what's the what are some of the reduced minimal market set sizes that replicate say the trend following industry
claims.claim: A reduced, minimal set of markets is enough to replicate the trend-following industry, and replication ETFs' changes to their market set over time made little difference.
claims.testable: yes - tracking error vs number of markets in a trend replication

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: if we do replicate the replicators we actually end up with better performance but that's probably not too surprising because we end up with a little better smoothing coefficient and we have probably end up with less churn for rebalances
claims.claim: Replicating the replication products with better smoothing and less rebalancing churn (plus lower fees and better cash management if fully funded) beats the retail replication products.
claims.conditions: for large institutions running it themselves
claims.testable: yes - compare smoothed low-turnover replication vs ETF returns net of costs

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: are two failure points for some of the professional allocation stabs that exist in the world.
claims.claim: Overall cost and manager selection risk are the two main failure points of professional allocators, which is why replication products appeal.
claims.testable: partly - dispersion of manager returns and fee drag measurable

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: non-trending periods are also behavioral and the periods of high liquidity are behavioral and the periods of low liquidity are behavioral because the markets are the some of the participant behaviors
claims.claim: Trends, non-trending periods and liquidity regimes are all behavioral because markets are the sum of participant behavior, so a behavioral explanation of trends must also explain their absence.
claims.testable: no - interpretive

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: I think one can decompose returns into the components of economic trend into financial carry into information diffusion and then into some form of reflexivity in a sorosian term
claims.claim: Trend-following returns (holding positions through time while buying strength and selling weakness) decompose into economic carry, financial carry, information diffusion and reflexive feedback, each with different strength by sector and different time scales.
claims.indicator: economic carry; financial carry; information diffusion; reflexivity
claims.conditions: component weights vary by sector and horizon
claims.testable: yes - attribute trend returns to carry and residual price-momentum components

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: have a positive positive economic carry, for instance, in equity indices, which is extremely strong, but have faced for most of the time a negative financial carry and still come
claims.claim: In equity index futures a strong positive economic carry (growth) has outweighed a mostly negative financial carry, so the return components can point in opposite directions and still net positive.
claims.indicator: equity index futures financial carry (roll/basis) vs economic carry
claims.direction: long equity indices net positive despite negative carry
claims.testable: yes - split equity futures returns into roll yield and spot

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: if one does a pretty careful decomposition of trend, one will find that the majority and in some cases the vast majority of returns will be accumulated term structure premia.
claims.claim: In fixed income futures, which have little economic carry but strong financial (roll) carry, most of trend following's return is accumulated term structure premia.
claims.indicator: bond futures roll premium / term structure
claims.conditions: fixed income; not true in other markets
claims.testable: yes - decompose bond-futures trend P&L into roll and spot

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: everyone everyone was writing how much bonds will go up and how much interest rates will go up and to get ready. And of course what happened in 2014 interest rates went down the entire year
claims.claim: In 2013 the consensus expected rising rates, but rates fell all of 2014 and trend followers made 20-30%, showing agnostic trend capture beats consensus forecasts.
claims.testable: yes - check 2014 trend returns and rate path vs 2013 forecasts

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: They get why the correlation is zero. They get why it's positively convex.
claims.claim: Return attribution of trend into its components explains its roughly zero correlation to traditional assets and its positive convexity.
claims.testable: partly - correlation and convexity measurable; explanatory link is interpretive

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: So if I make something shortterm I'm essentially taking those out of the equation.
claims.claim: Carry returns accrue with holding time, so short holding periods remove the economic and financial carry components and leave mostly information diffusion and reflexivity.
claims.testable: yes - carry share of trend P&L by lookback/holding period

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: these kinds of these kinds of more market mechanistic I think are far more useful in the time frames s of say less than 10day holding periods.
claims.claim: For holding periods under about 10 days, flow effects (accelerating, periodic and rebalancing flows) are the more useful return sources.
claims.testable: yes - rebalancing/flow calendar signals at short horizons

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: very few instances except for very large contracts, large dollar volatility of the contracts, oftentimes with large point values in those contracts where you can parameterize any type of a traditional trend following mechanistic approach
claims.claim: Traditional trend following rarely makes money with 3-5 day holding periods (except in very large, high dollar-volatility contracts) because little profit is left between buying strength and selling weakness; academic short-term trend still holds about a month.
claims.indicator: trend signal with 3-5 day holding period
claims.conditions: fails at very short holdings except large high dollar-vol contracts
claims.testable: yes - net-of-cost trend returns by holding period and contract size

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: Trend uses price. The macro trading uses only cross asset signals, fundamental signals, government reports, alternative data.
claims.claim: Keeping a full separation of inputs between sleeves (trend on price only, systematic macro on fundamental/cross-asset/alternative data only, short-term on flows) gives distinct return sources.
claims.indicator: price; cross-asset, fundamental, government and alternative data; flows
claims.testable: yes - correlation between sleeves built on separate inputs

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: there's a natural construction where you can build say a dollarneutral currency basket now you're not stacking on top of your dollar risk
claims.claim: Relative-value baskets neutralized to the main thematic risks (dollar-neutral FX, rate-neutral rates, commodity-neutral commodities) add diversification without stacking on the main portfolio's directional risk.
claims.indicator: dollar, DV01 and commodity beta neutrality
claims.conditions: when the main portfolio holds large thematic directional risks
claims.testable: yes - neutral basket returns and their correlation with the directional book

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: the fifth thing that we do in our multistrategy is a dedicated risk off sleeve which is only designed to sell equities when there's a rapid rise in flow data that shows us to have hedging and mispricing activities
claims.claim: A dedicated risk-off sleeve shorts equities only when flow data show a rapid rise in hedging demand, because hedgers pay to offload risk and that raises the edge.
claims.indicator: flow data showing hedging activity / mispricing
claims.conditions: only on a rapid rise in hedging flows
claims.testable: partly - needs hedging-flow data (e.g. options/futures positioning)

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: all investors if we looked at a hundred trillion dollars in allocatable capital around the world are massively underallocated to alternatives not over.
claims.claim: Globally, investors are heavily underallocated to alternatives, so multistrategy growth is a positive for investors.
claims.indicator: global allocatable capital (~$100tn) share in alternatives
claims.testable: partly - allocation data exist; optimal share is a judgement

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: no, not at all. The I think the majority of hedge or of trend following returns are have been driven by accumulated economic and financial carries and information diffusion over months if not semianual
claims.claim: The rise of large multistrategy funds has not made trend following harder, because trend returns come from carries and information diffusion over months to years rather than the short-term microstructure multistrats trade.
claims.testable: partly - trend returns vs multistrat AUM growth over time

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: It's definitely affected when spreads from in G7 environments all become extremely narrow and there's virtually no difference. These are these are massive differences for trend following.
claims.claim: Zero-interest-rate policy and very narrow G7 rate spreads remove financial carry and hurt trend-following returns.
claims.indicator: policy rate level (ZIRP); G7 interest rate spreads
claims.direction: lower trend returns when rates near zero and spreads narrow
claims.testable: yes - trend returns conditional on rate level and cross-country rate dispersion

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: if if anything for most trend followers it's either not seen or it may even be providing a liquidity pool.
claims.claim: High-leverage short-term arbitrage and stat-arb trading by multistrats operates in market microstructure that trend followers do not see, and may even provide them liquidity.
claims.testable: partly - trend execution costs before/after multistrat growth

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: And I think then when you get to people who are living in a world where very adverse moves that occur over quarters or or years matter to them. trend following becomes this invaluable tool if they use it right.
claims.claim: For institutions where multi-quarter or multi-year adverse moves create large liabilities (e.g. two-sigma pension shortfalls), trend following is a key strategic tail-cover allocation, unlike a pure own-everything view.
claims.direction: allocate to trend for tail cover
claims.conditions: slow adverse moves over quarters or years
claims.testable: yes - trend returns during multi-quarter equity/bond drawdowns

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: This whole narrative that a trend follower can get too big and somehow their returns will go away. No, not if they compensate for it by the same thought experiment.
claims.claim: Aggregate industry size (about $250bn) does not by itself erode trend returns: a single owner of $200bn run as many independent managers would perform the same, so capacity is solved by diversifying approaches.
claims.conditions: if size is spread across many distinct approaches
claims.testable: partly - trend returns vs industry AUM

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: You could end up running hundreds of different kinds of systematic approaches and at some point you will become average.
claims.claim: Diversifying across very many systematic approaches converges to the industry average, giving up any edge over the industry.
claims.indicator: number of approaches vs correlation to industry index
claims.testable: yes - correlation to CTA index as number of combined systems grows

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: less so I think in long-term trend following than in other categories we could talk about that are more sensitive to capacity.
claims.claim: Some managers have overstepped capacity, but long-term trend following is less capacity-sensitive than other strategy categories.
claims.testable: partly - market impact by strategy holding period

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: they would be fighting the impression of style drift or of changing what they're doing in front of their clients.
claims.claim: Managers who need to diversify methods to handle more assets face clients' style-drift concerns, so such changes take years and fast asset raising makes capacity problems likely.
claims.testable: no - business dynamics

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: a large volume of dollars trying to go in a into a smaller market more rapidly is going to press a market and cause a capacity issue
claims.claim: Market impact rises with dollars traded relative to market size and with trading speed; liquidity is dynamic by time of day and market, so small slow trades in large markets do not move prices.
claims.indicator: trade size vs market liquidity; trading speed
claims.conditions: liquidity varies by time of day and market
claims.testable: yes - impact models vs participation rate

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: if people are very diligent about seeing the fingerprint of their execution costs and their execution alpha and they begin to see their execution costs rise objectively measured
claims.claim: A capacity problem shows up as an upward trend in objectively measured execution costs (and falling execution alpha), usually in a few markets long before all markets.
claims.indicator: execution costs / slippage and execution alpha by market
claims.conditions: appears first in a few markets
claims.testable: yes - track slippage trend by market vs AUM

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: you could trade that much in copper but you can't trade that much in tin and you're going to have to decide how to accommodate for that.
claims.claim: Capacity differs by market (e.g. copper vs tin), and rising costs must be judged as temporary illiquidity (a country or currency that recovers within months) or too much money for that market.
claims.conditions: illiquid markets; temporary vs structural illiquidity
claims.testable: yes - per-market liquidity caps and their effect on returns

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: If you have one that if you delay by 15 minutes, you lose 20% of your P&L, you have one that's pretty time-sensitive.
claims.claim: Strategies whose results change a lot when execution is delayed are time-sensitive, more exposed to microstructure and capacity, and have less margin of error out of sample than delay-insensitive long-holding strategies.
claims.testable: yes - rerun backtests with delayed execution

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: they can't figure out why sometimes this amount of unemployment report change had this big of a market move and other
claims.claim: The market response to a given data surprise (e.g. unemployment) is unstable because data do not trade, people do; modelling data-to-price as a fixed two-body relation misleads early quants.
claims.testable: yes - rolling price response to data surprises

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: when I first started trading the M1, M2 and M3 money supply used to be on the front page of the Wall Street Journal and because everybody followed money supply.
claims.claim: Regimes include which information markets care about: money supply once drove markets and is now ignored, so indicator importance shifts over time.
claims.conditions: importance of an indicator varies by era
claims.testable: yes - time-varying market response to money supply releases

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: you might want to trade differently in a high inflation, you know, rising interest rate, supply constrained world than you might want to do in a demand constrained, low interest rate, low inflation world.
claims.claim: Strategy should be conditioned on the macro regime (high inflation, rising rates, supply-constrained vs low inflation, low rates, demand-constrained) as a setup, not as a precise prediction.
claims.indicator: inflation level; interest rate direction; supply vs demand constraint
claims.testable: yes - strategy returns conditional on inflation/rate regimes

claims.speaker: Pat Welton
claims.quote: the return gap the negative investor alpha that occurs from people switching on performance is is usually the biggest cost that they face in putting their portfolios together
claims.claim: Steady holding compounds best; the return gap from switching managers or strategies on recent performance is usually investors' largest cost.
claims.testable: yes - dollar-weighted vs time-weighted fund returns
